title: The big lookout
hook: year one is done; ahead lie the ranges: the daily banis, the long story, the ways of the Guru, the Granth itself

segments.voice: Yesterday, the good of all: every Ardas ends by asking good for everyone, sarbat da bhala, and your line, for everyone, not just us. Today is the last day of year one. Day three hundred thirty-one.

Near the top of a long hike, tired legs earn a stop. A hiker turns around, and there it is: the whole valley walked through, small and golden below. Then the other way: more mountains. Bigger ones, blue in the distance. Two thoughts can arrive at once on a spot like that. I made it. And, look how much more there is. This is that spot, the last day of year one. Today: the big lookout.
screen: `A TIRED HIKER TURNS AROUND.` → `THE VALLEY BEHIND, SMALL AND GOLDEN.` → `MORE MOUNTAINS AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Start with the word Sikh itself. It is usually traced to an old Indian word for a student, a disciple, a learner. Sikhs often put it simply: a Sikh is someone who keeps learning from the Guru. Not someone who finishes. So a year of learning doesn't end with a diploma. It ends at a lookout. Turn around first. You began with first words: seva, Waheguru, Ik Onkar, langar, sangat. Then the stories: ten Gurus, one light. Then the practices: kirtan, simran, Nitnem, a visit to the gurdwara. Then the Japji, pauri by pauri, all thirty-eight and the saloks. Then the depths: the Granth's great themes, Kabir and Farid, the rehat, the history, and the grief of 1984 carried carefully. That's the valley. Now turn and face the other way. Four ranges stand out there. First, the daily banis: Jaap Sahib tomorrow, then Anand Sahib, Rehras, Kirtan Sohila, Sukhmani, the prayers many Sikhs say morning and evening. Then the long story: Sikh history told slowly, century by century. Then the ways of the Guru: how Sikhs live it, day to day. And then the Granth itself, fourteen hundred thirty pages, the Guru Sikhs bow to. Daunting? Sikhs have a phrase for the spirit to meet it with, and you met it on day seventeen: chardi kala. Rising spirits. An unbeaten, upward-facing mind. It sits in the very last line of the Ardas, right beside the good of all from yesterday. Chardi kala isn't pretending things are easy. The Sikh story has plenty of hard days in it, and this year's path passed through some of them. It's facing forward anyway, in good heart, because the road is long and the company is good. That's the lookout: grateful behind, awake ahead.
screen: `SIKH: A LEARNER WHO KEEPS LEARNING.` · `THE VALLEY: WORDS, STORIES, PRACTICES, DEPTHS.` · `THE RANGES: BANIS, STORY, WAYS, GRANTH.` · `CHARDI KALA: FACE FORWARD, IN GOOD HEART.` · then, large: `WOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look out a window. Find one, any one, and let your eyes go as far as they can. A rooftop, a tree, a strip of sky. Breathe slowly. For the first part, think back over the year: one word, one story, one practice that stayed with you. Then let your gaze go farther, to the edge of what you can see, and just notice that there is more out there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru under your breath, the Sikh word of wonder you met in camp one. If you don't, simply stay with what you see. The bell holds the time.
The big lookout. The top of year one: the valley of words, stories, practices and depths behind you, and the ranges of the banis and the Granth ahead, met in chardi kala.
Your line: wow. Today, catch one moment that earns it, a sky, a kindness, a sentence that lands, and actually say it. Day three hundred thirty-one. Year one, done.

screen: `DAY 331 COUNTS.` → `YEAR ONE, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: THE TENTH GURU'S MORNING PRAISE.`

howItsDone: Sikhs often describe themselves as lifelong learners of the Guru, and the Ardas said at the close of gurdwara gatherings ends by asking for chardi kala, rising spirits, and the good of all.

match.prompt: the big lookout — tap the pairs.

myth: the word Sikh means someone who has finished learning
it is usually traced to an old word for a student or disciple: a Sikh keeps learning from the Guru.
chardi kala means pretending everything is fine
it's facing forward in good heart even on hard days, not denying them.
chardi kala appears in the last line of the Ardas
it sits beside the request for the good of all, sarbat da bhala.

fork.setup: you've climbed a whole year of the path and reached the lookout. what does the word Sikh suggest comes next?
options: stop here: the learning is complete.
keep walking: a Sikh is a learner for life.
go back to the bottom and start over.
fork.reveal: the word Sikh is usually traced to a word for a learner or disciple. the lookout isn't the end of the road; ahead lie the daily banis, the long story, the ways of the Guru and the Granth itself.

original.note: Gurmukhi: chardi kala, rising spirits; the mood Sikhs meet the road ahead with, named in the Ardas's last line.

trapdoor: what you thought: a year of lessons ends at a finish line.
what it means: it ends at a lookout, grateful for the valley behind and awake to the ranges ahead, in chardi kala.
what a scholar hears: Sikh is usually traced to Sanskrit shishya, disciple (compare Pali sikkha, training); Sikhs read the name as a learner for life.

sources.ref: Ardas, closing line (chardi kala and sarbat da bhala)
sources.work: Ardas, as given in the Sikh Rehat Maryada (SGPC)

notes: Year one close. The look-back list (first words, stories, practices, Japji, depths including 1984) summarizes camps 1–5; confirm it fairly represents the year.
Etymology of 'Sikh' from Sanskrit shishya (disciple), with Pali sikkha as a related form: confirm wording.
Chardi kala is placed in the last line of the Ardas beside sarbat da bhala; Gurmukhi ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ and pronunciation CHUR-dee KA-laa to be checked.

The four ranges ahead (daily banis, the long story, the ways of the Guru, the Granth itself) follow the outline for years two to five; the year-two bani list (Jaap Sahib, Anand Sahib, Rehras, Kirtan Sohila, Sukhmani) follows y2.md.
Chardi kala was camp one's word on day fifteen; the teach refers back to it.
